item.title: Man films himself taking down Flock cameras, gets arrested
item.description: Jevon Martinez livestreamed himself removing 10 Flock Safety cameras in Bernalillo County, but authorities say eight belonged to neighborhood associations.
item.content:encoded:
You might expect someone taking down surveillance cameras to avoid being filmed. Jevon Martinez did the opposite.

The 44-year-old Rio Rancho, New Mexico, man recorded himself removing Flock Safety camera equipment around Bernalillo County on Sept. 2. He loaded the equipment into his pickup truck while explaining his reasoning to people watching online. The timing gave Martinez his opening.

Days earlier, Bernalillo County Sheriff John Allen had moved to end the department's three contracts with Flock Safety. Allen cited concerns about privacy, data sharing and his confidence in the company. However, he still supports automated license plate reader technology and plans to look at other vendors.

Martinez apparently saw the remaining cameras as unfinished business. What happened next shows how quickly a fight over surveillance can turn into a criminal case once someone starts removing hardware they do not own.

No technical experience is needed.

TEENS ACCUSED OF DESTROYING FLOCK CAMERA UNTIL BATTERY EXPLODED, IGNITING FIRE NEAR HOMES: REPORT

Martinez made his position unusually easy to understand because he documented it himself. In a Sept. 2 social media post, Martinez said BCSO no longer subscribed to Flock. He wrote that he was taking down the equipment so he could return it.

He also insisted that he was neither destroying nor stealing the equipment. Martinez described it as property that had been left unattended.

His videos carried the same message. "Since BCSO is busy, I know BCSO is busy, everyone who works for BCSO, I know you guys are busy, so I went ahead and helped you out," Martinez says while driving his pickup.

The camera then shows what he means by "helped." His truck bed is filling up with Flock equipment.

This also was not Martinez's first encounter with law enforcement over license plate readers. Rio Rancho police had arrested him months earlier in a separate Sandoval County case involving the alleged removal and damage of three license plate reader systems. He faced nine felony charges in that case.

Martinez does not come across in the videos as someone trying to keep a low profile. Quite the opposite. "We got a bunch of these bad boys," he says while showing off the equipment in the back of the truck.

Then comes the line that gives the videos an almost game-like quality. "Let's see how much I can get in one day. That's gonna be the challenge for everyone out there."

At another point, Martinez tells viewers, "Not in my city, not in my state." He also repeatedly calls the Flock cameras "tyranny trees," a nickname that says plenty about how he views automated vehicle surveillance. Reports of his livestream show him dismantling one of the systems while continuing to explain his position. Martinez creates his own record as he goes, with his face, voice and actions captured on camera.

This is where Martinez's social media explanation runs into an important problem. Bernalillo County authorities say he removed 10 Flock camera systems with an estimated combined value of $16,500.

However, only two were associated with BCSO. Authorities say the other eight were managed by neighborhood associations. That changes the picture considerably.

Martinez repeatedly described what he was doing as returning equipment to the sheriff after BCSO ended its relationship with Flock. Yet most of the systems authorities recovered were connected to other organizations.

BCSO also says the equipment remained property that members of the public had no authorization to remove. So while Martinez's videos clearly explain what he believed he was doing, they do not settle the ownership question.

EX-INDIANA DEPUTY CHARGED WITH FELONY FOR ALLEGEDLY USING FLOCK CAMERAS TO STALK GIRLFRIEND

Martinez said throughout his videos that he planned to return the equipment to BCSO. However, investigators give a somewhat different account of how that ended.

According to the criminal complaint, Martinez drove past BCSO headquarters three times while the equipment remained in his truck. Deputies eventually stopped him outside the sheriff's office.

Video of the arrest shows deputies surrounding his pickup with guns drawn before placing him in handcuffs. Martinez was unarmed, and the charges against him stem from the alleged removal of the equipment rather than a violent offense.

Court reporting differs slightly on the precise larceny charge. One account of the criminal complaint describes attempted larceny over $2,500, while BCSO reporting lists larceny over $2,500. He also faces an interference with communications charge.

Martinez appeared virtually in Bernalillo County Metropolitan Court on Sept. 4. Prosecutors did not file a pretrial detention motion, and Judge Claire McDaniel did not order him held in the Bernalillo County case.

That did not mean Martinez walked free. He remained in custody because of the separate Sandoval County case tied to the earlier alleged license plate reader removals. Reports say that Sandoval County held him over a violation of his release conditions and that a grand jury has since indicted him in that case. The cases remain unresolved, and the charges are allegations unless and until proven in court.

There is another wrinkle here that makes this story more interesting. Sheriff Allen had already reached his own breaking point with Flock Safety.

BCSO had three contracts connected to the company. One covered five automatic license plate reader cameras. Another involved 16 speed cameras connected to the Flock network. A third covered gunshot detection technology.

Allen said he had lost confidence in Flock over privacy safeguards and data sharing. He also raised concerns about other law enforcement agencies gaining access to New Mexico plate data.

Still, Allen has defended the underlying technology as a useful law enforcement tool. His disagreement centers on the vendor and the safeguards surrounding the data. That puts BCSO and Martinez in an unusual position. Both expressed serious concerns about Flock. Their ideas about what should happen next could hardly be further apart.

Automatic license plate readers can create a detailed record of where vehicles appear. Flock's LPR systems collect license plate text along with the date, time and camera location. They can also record basic vehicle characteristics such as make, model and color. Flock says the system does not collect the driver's identity through the LPR camera.

Police can use that information to generate leads in investigations. The concern comes from what happens when millions of those observations become searchable.

We saw the risks firsthand in Colorado, where a woman faced a porch theft accusation after Flock cameras linked her truck to the area. Other location data eventually helped her show where she actually was.

Flock cameras have also moved into places you may visit every week. CyberGuy found license plate readers operating at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots in Connecticut. That means pulling into a store can create another record tied to your vehicle.

Then there are systems that can combine different types of signals. We recently looked at SignalTrace, technology that can correlate wireless device signals with license plate reader information and travel patterns.

All of this helps explain why a camera on a roadside can trigger such a strong reaction. It does not give someone permission to dismantle one.

You can question automatic license plate readers without ever touching a camera. Start by finding out which company operates the readers in your community and how long your local agency keeps the data.

Then ask who can search the system and how officials audit those searches. Private cameras deserve attention too. A homeowners association, shopping center or business may operate plate readers that connect with law enforcement.

Public records can help you understand how local agencies use the technology. Public meetings also give residents a way to challenge contracts before officials renew them.

If you want cameras removed, push the people who have the legal authority to make that decision. That keeps the debate focused on surveillance policy rather than turning it into a criminal case.

TENNESSEE OFFICIAL SAYS FLOCK CEO SHOULD BE HANGED 'PUBLICLY FOR TREASON’ AS CONTROVERSIAL CAMERAS FACE REVOLT

I understand why these cameras make people uncomfortable. A system that quietly logs where vehicles appear deserves close scrutiny, especially when information can move between agencies. Bernalillo County's own sheriff had enough concerns about Flock to walk away from the company. Martinez clearly shares the privacy concern, but his videos show what can happen when someone decides to take the next step on his own. 

The biggest factual problem with his argument is hard to overlook. Authorities say only two of the 10 systems he removed were associated with BCSO. The other eight were managed by neighborhood associations. Then there are the videos themselves. Martinez wanted people to see what he was doing. He explained his reasoning and showed the equipment piling up in his truck. Those posts may help him make a political argument online. They also give investigators a remarkably detailed record of what happened. For me, the useful questions are who gets to collect our movement data and what limits control access to it. Those are fights worth having in public.

If your local sheriff said it no longer trusted a surveillance company, would you want every camera removed immediately or would you accept a replacement system with stronger privacy safeguards? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

item.title: Coastal town revolts after $9.5M upgrade walls off beloved ocean views: 'You can't see the sea'
item.description: A California state agency agreed to modify a tall new fence in Fort Bragg after residents said it blocks their beloved Noyo Headlands ocean views.
item.content:encoded:
A California state agency is changing its construction plans following an outcry from residents who said a new fence was blocking the town’s ocean views.

The California Department of Transportation’s (Caltrans) approximately $9.5 million improvement project was undertaken to address pedestrian safety and disability access along Highway 1 through Fort Bragg in Northern California’s Mendocino County.

But as soon as residents saw a tall new fence start to go up, they took action.

ONCE-HIDDEN COASTAL TOWN FACING DISRUPTION AS SOCIAL MEDIA INFLUENCERS TRANSFORM LOCAL LIFE

"The entrance to our town now has a fence that is substantially higher than the original fence and blocks the view of the ocean — a view that has long been part of what makes Fort Bragg special," Mary Rose Kaczorowski, a candidate for Fort Bragg City Council, wrote in a letter to the editor of the Ukiah Daily Journal.

"This is not simply a matter of replacing an existing fence; it changes the character and view of one of our town’s important gateways," she wrote.

The new fence along Main Street replaced an older, shorter wooden fence that allowed passersby to see the Noyo Headlands and ocean beyond it, according to SFGATE.

"We’re marketing towards being a sea town, but you can’t see the sea. It’s a bit of a buzzkill," Aiden McFadden, a front-desk associate at the Seabird Lodge, told SFGATE.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We understand why they’re putting in the fencing, but we didn’t expect there to be an actual wall, a barrier, between us and the ocean view," she said. "The original fence did its work."

Kaczorowski wrote that residents and "everyone who comes to Fort Bragg" deserved "a clear explanation of why this substantially higher fence was installed and how the decision was made."

"Did anyone stop to ask how this substantially higher fence would affect the people who live here — or how it would change the view at the entrance to our town?" she wrote. "That is precisely why coastal local residents are shocked and angry at the fence that blocks our coastal view."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Caltrans held an open house for public comment on the project in April.

In August, Fort Bragg City Manager Isaac Whippy announced in a news release that the city had heard the community’s concerns regarding the new wooden fencing’s height, appearance and impact on views.

"The fencing is part of Caltrans’ Fort Bragg sidewalk and Americans with Disabilities Act improvement project," Whippy explained. "It replaced an existing fence that was removed to accommodate sidewalk widening and accessibility improvements. The fence and its associated construction costs are components of Caltrans’ broader project contract and are not a separate City construction project."

After residents raised concerns, "City staff reviewed the permit and related project documents, which indicate that the replacement fencing was intended to match the previous conditions," the release further stated.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Whippy said he spoke directly with the project manager, who was "receptive to the concerns raised by the community and has expressed a strong commitment to working with the City and Caltrans’ contractor to identify and implement appropriate modifications."

"We have a timeline for the construction crew to come back to town in the next couple of weeks for fence modifications," Whippy told SFGATE.

item.title: Judge Judy preparing to end decades-long run as TV's toughest judge
item.description: Judge Judy Sheindlin reveals she's retiring from TV after "Judy Justice" ends in October, but her next move keeps her in the entertainment world.
item.content:encoded:
Judge Judy Sheindlin is planning to hang up her robe for good.

"Judge Judy is passing the gavel to her son, Adam Levy, in ‘Adam’s Law,'the courtroom program she created and is an executive producer," a rep for Sheindlin told Fox News Digital. "It premieres in national syndication this Monday, Sept. 14."

"She is not retiring, just rewiring."

During a recent interview with People, the 83-year-old judge and television personality shared that she plans on retiring from TV after her Prime Video series, "Judy Justice," comes to an end in October.

"I have a lot of other things of interest," she said. "I don’t want to do hair and makeup anymore, but I still want my message to get out there."

ROSIE O'DONNELL WALKED AWAY AT THE HEIGHT OF HER SUCCESS AFTER REACHING ONE JAW-DROPPING FINANCIAL MILESTONE

Her son, Levy, graduated from New York’s Hofstra Law School, and after taking a detour working as a ski instructor, he worked in private practice and as the Putnam County, N.Y., district attorney, before starting his own journey in television in 2023 on the Prime Video show "Tribunal Justice."

"There aren’t a lot of people who can carry a half hour on their own unscripted," Sheindlin said. "He has what it takes."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Sheindlin graduated from New York Law School in 1965 and worked as a prosecutor, handling juvenile crime, domestic violence and child-abuse cases, starting in 1972.

After retiring from family court, she launched the popular syndicated show "Judge Judy," which aired for 25 seasons, from 1996 to 2021. At its peak, the show reached an estimated 10 million viewers, and Sheindlin became known for her no-nonsense attitude and classic one-liners.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"So many of the emails and letters I get are from women who watched me and had their daughters watch me," she told the LA Times in June 2021 about the impact of the show. "They told me the show helped them take the next step, whether it was getting a divorce, leaving an abusive person, asking for a raise and never, ever becoming somebody’s prisoner."

During an interview with Fox News Digital in November 2022, Sheindlin's granddaughter, Sarah Rose, shared what her grandmother taught her, noting she does in fact have a soft side despite her TV persona. 

She shared that the best piece of advice Sheindlin has given her is that "you have to define yourself, and you tell other people who you are. Not the other way around."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"[She taught me] not to let anybody else define you but yourself," Sarah Rose said. "You have to have a good feeling about yourself and be confident in yourself. And, really, if you have that as a foundation, the opportunities are endless for where your journey might lead. I’ve always taken that to heart. No matter what anyone else’s opinions, feelings or thoughts are, I just know that I’m secure in myself. And she’s playing a big role in that."

While Sara Rose admits Sheindlin could be a "no-nonsense grandmother," she also has "a much softer, supportive side," noting she is often "the first person I call if I have a problem or a question or something that needs to get solved."

"She’s a fantastic problem solver, especially for the ones that she loves," she added.

item.title: Dem handlers lash out when Ramaswamy staffer confronts their boss about debate: ‘No pictures’
item.description: Video shows Amy Acton's campaign staff confronting a cameraman who asked why she refuses to debate Vivek Ramaswamy in the Ohio governor race.
item.content:encoded:
Campaign personnel for Amy Acton, Ohio’s former health director and Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, got into a confrontation with a Republican political activist wielding a camera last Saturday at one of Acton’s campaign events in Harrison, Ohio.

When the cameraman approached Acton, asking her why she continued to decline invitations to debate her Republican challenger, Vivek Ramaswamy, her staff quickly rushed in to block him off from Acton.

The video, which shows Acton walking away from the interviewer, adds to criticisms from Ramaswamy’s camp that she hasn’t given a good answer for why she isn’t willing to do a debate as both candidates enter the homestretch of their campaigns.

RAMASWAMY PUMPS $25M OF OWN CASH INTO OHIO GOVERNOR BID, SMASHES FUNDRAISING RECORDS WITH $50 MILLION HAUL

"Dr. Amy Acton, why do you refuse to debate your opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy?" the interviewer asked.

"No photos, no videos," the staff repeated. "I said — no pictures, no interviews."

At one point in the confrontation, Acton’s staff seemed to have bumped into the cameraman, jolting his camera out of frame and prompting him to ask them to be "careful."

Acton did not respond to the questions.

Earlier this month, after Ramaswamy accepted a debate invitation from CNN, Acton’s campaign told local media she would not accept.

"Dr. Acton’s focus is on talking with Ohioans, not platforming a scam artist who spreads baseless lies about her and her family, uses AI to falsely paint her as someone with a substance abuse problem, and shames Dr. Acton for being sexually abused as a child while Vivek stands with predators and abusers," a campaign spokesperson said in a Sept. 2 statement.

ARMED MAN ACCUSED OF LUNGING AT OHIO DEM CANDIDATE AVOIDS FELONIES AS PROSECUTOR REVEALS KEY EVIDENCE

TOP ELECTION SCHEMES ROILING KEY MIDTERM RACES AS BOTH PARTIES ACCUSE RIVALS OF TRICKERY

The response refers to a series of Republican attacks: her role in Ohio’s COVID response, a verbal domestic dispute in 2019 that she had while intoxicated, and AI-generated campaign ads that replaced her car’s license plate with a "drunk mom" tag. It also nods to Ramaswamy’s quiet posture toward releasing the Epstein files at the outset of his gubernatorial campaign.

In his response, Ramaswamy ignored Acton’s needling.

He seized on her decision, calling into question her qualifications to lead the state as its top executive while, at the same time, refusing to press her case on a debate stage.

"It’s too bad for Ohio voters that Acton won’t take voter questions, won’t debate, quit after failing as Ohio’s health director, and has some serious issues now surfaced in multiple police reports," Ramaswamy said in a post to social media.

FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE

Acton’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital about her interaction with the interviewer last Saturday.

Having cleared the Ohio Democratic primary, Acton will face off against Ramaswamy in the state’s general election on Nov. 3.

item.title: Intel chief warns of 'evolving' threats as terror groups now 'recruit their agents online'
item.description: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warns terrorists now recruit online, citing an alleged ISIS bomb plot near New York City's Gracie Mansion.
item.content:encoded:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned about the growing threat global terror organizations pose to the United States through their ability to radicalize individuals online at home.

Speaking on "Special Report," Clayton pointed to an attempted bombing in New York City as an example of how modern extremists no longer need distant foreign training camps to launch attacks and instead can be recruited online.

Clayton responded after host Bret Baier cited United Nations figures showing that al Qaeda's global network has grown to an estimated 25,000 potential fighters — roughly 50 times its estimated size at the time of the Sept. 11 terror attacks in 2001.

TOP HOUSE CHAIRMAN WARNS CONGRESS AGAINST 'COMPLACENCY' 25 YEARS AFTER 9/11

"Those numbers may be surprising. I think it's important for America to hear those numbers, but they reflect the evolving threat environment, the threat environment from terrorists," Clayton told Baier.

"Terrorists recruit today much differently than they did 25 years ago," he said.

AMERICAN 'JIHAD' FUELED BY 'RISKY SOURCE' INSIDE US BORDERS, WARNS NATIONAL SECURITY EXPERT

Clayton said terrorists were previously often recruited and trained in camps overseas, but that process has changed in the 25 years since 9/11.

"Today, they recruit their agents online. They attempt to radicalize them online," Clayton said.

KASH PATEL REVEALS THE CHILLING HOLIDAY TERROR PLOTS FBI FEDERAL AGENTS QUIETLY STOPPED

"Just this year, we had two radicalized men from Pennsylvania travel to New York to try and detonate a bomb outside Gracie Mansion. Thanks to the NYPD, who just like in 9/11 ran to the fire, no one was killed," he added.

Federal prosecutors described both men as supporters of ISIS who consumed radical content online.

Prosecutors allege the men traveled from Pennsylvania to Manhattan on March 7 with two explosive devices and attempted to detonate them near protesters and police officers outside Gracie Mansion, the official residence of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

EXCLUSIVE: 25 YEARS AFTER 9/11, ICE SAYS MORE THAN 2K KNOWN OR SUSPECTED TERRORISTS HAVE BEEN DEPORTED

When asked about remaining security gaps identified in a recent House Intelligence Committee report, Clayton said communication among intelligence and law enforcement agencies has improved significantly since 9/11.

"What I can tell you is that the women and men of the intelligence community, working domestically with law enforcement, working overseas with our partners, are committed every day to closing those gaps and identifying evolving threats," Clayton said.

"There have been, and again, the American people should know this, there have been many threats on our soil that have been thwarted," he added.

item.title: Blue state governor's pardon of convicted felon torpedos a major Supreme Court immigration fight
item.description: Kathy Hochul pardoned a convicted noncitizen, effectively mooting a Supreme Court case on bond hearing rights for detained immigrants facing deportation.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court will no longer hear an oral argument for a case centered on bond rights for noncitizens detained for lengthy periods, ruling the case moot after New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul pardoned a lawfully present Dominican citizen, who pleaded guilty to second-degree assault.

Hochul pardoned Keisy Guerrero Mariano, who is identified in court documents as "Keisy GM," in late August, effectively killing the Trump administration's appeal to the Supreme Court arguing that noncitizens, including those with green card status, do not have a legal right to a bond hearing for a prolonged detention if they have committed crimes that are grounds for mandatory deportation.

Hochul, who is staunchly opposed to President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement crackdown, issued the pardon for Mariano just as the brief was due.

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT

Solicitor General John Sauer agreed Friday that Genalo v. Black is now moot, but said the Trump administration will seek an "alternative vehicle" to challenge the Second Circuit’s 2024 ruling that prolonged immigration detention can trigger a constitutional right to a bond hearing.

Sauer said the administration intends to find another case through which the Supreme Court can resolve the issue during its 2026-27 term.

The lawsuit centered on the challenges of plaintiffs Carol Williams Black, a Jamaican national with lawful standing, and Mariano — both convicted criminals detained by ICE.

APPEALS COURT BLOCKS TRUMP ADMIN FROM HOLDING MIGRANTS WITHOUT BOND FOR OVER 90 DAYS

Mariano was first arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in 2020 over a 2015 second-degree assault conviction for which he served time, making him eligible for deportation.

He spent nearly two years in ICE detention, but was released in 2022 due to a nationwide injunction that required the release of detainees because of COVID-19 health risks.

Prior to his release, Judge John P. Cronan of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York denied Mariano's habeas corpus request in November 2021.

But in May 2024, the Second Circuit overruled Cronan's decision, ruling that the government must grant noncitizens a bond hearing once detention becomes "unreasonably long." Failure to do so, the court ruled, would violate the Fifth Amendment's due process clause.

The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case June 15; however, the high court ruled Black's case moot because he had left the United States and filed a court declaration that he would not be returning to the country.

Black was convicted in New York in 2000 of sexually abusing a minor under the age of 11.

DHS BLASTS MINNESOTA BOARD FOR UNANIMOUSLY PARDONING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CONVICTED OF 3 ASSAULTS

Hochul's decision to issue a pardon to Mariano has garnered fierce criticism from legal experts.

"Pretty wild to fully pardon an aggravated felon to (1) stop the felon from getting deported and (2) stop the Supreme Court from ruling on an issue. (Especially as this litigation has been going on for years)," Eric Wessan, Iowa’s solicitor general, posted on X.

He praised Sauer's decision to fight back on the Second Circuit's ruling.

"I wonder how many non-American felons Governors like Hochul will choose to fully pardon and free to avoid them facing consequences for their actions," Wessan added.

Fox News Digital reached out to Hochul's office for comment.

item.title: Ex-mayor found liable for alleged sexual assaults of 7 women, ordered to pay $13M
item.description: Dominic Foppoli, former Windsor, California, mayor, faces a punitive damages phase after a jury awarded seven women $13 million in sexual assault case.
item.content:encoded:
The former mayor of a small town in northern California was found civilly liable Friday for allegedly sexually assaulting seven women.

Dominic Foppoli, who led the town of Windsor from late 2018 to 2021, was ordered to pay a combined $13 million in compensatory damages. 

The payouts to the women, whose allegations span from 2001 to 2020, will range from $6,000 to $4,650,938 each, KTVU FOX 2 reported.

He could also have to pay punitive damages to the women. That phase of the civil trial will begin on Tuesday.

Foppoli has consistently denied all wrongdoing and has never been criminally charged in connection to the allegations. He stepped down as mayor in May 2021 after four women came forward to the San Francisco Chronicle to accuse him of sexual assault.

FORMER NJ DEM MAYOR ALLEGEDLY DRUGGED, SEXUALLY ASSAULTED CHILD HE MET ONLINE

The lawsuit, filed in April 2022, detailed allegations from seven Jane Does. Several women alleged Foppoli drugged their drinks before assaulting them, while Jane Doe 1 claimed he raped her dozens of times, including one alleged incident in which she said he handcuffed her to a bed.

According to the San Francisco Chronicle, a total of 13 women have accused Foppoli of sexual assault or misconduct.

In 2024, the state attorney general’s office suspended its criminal investigation into Foppoli, saying prosecutors did not have enough evidence to warrant filing charges on the cases not barred by the statute of limitations at that time.

Foppoli testified during the civil trial, which began in July, again denying the allegations against him.

"I've been a terrible boyfriend and partner, cheating, selfish and egotistical, but I've never done any of those things I'm being sued for," Foppoli said on the stand, according to KGO Eyewitness News.

The jury also found the Santa Rosa chapter of Active 20-30, an all-male charitable social club where Foppoli was a member, liable for Jane Doe 4's alleged assault and awarded her an additional $2 million, the Chronicle reported.

FBI AGENTS CONFRONT SWALWELL AT AIRPORT IN NEW FOOTAGE AS VIEWERS ZERO IN AND PILE ON

According to the lawsuit, the woman alleged Foppoli sexually assaulted her during the national Active 20-30 convention in Reno, Nevada, in June 2012. She also accused the organization of failing to investigate complaints she made to its leaders.

Traci Carrillo, an attorney for the plaintiffs, told Fox News Digital that the initial San Francisco Chronicle story "gave some of our clients a voice that no local news agency wanted to touch because it accused a powerful and connected local politician of crimes and sexual misconduct."

"It took over 5 years to get them justice, which was always about accountability. Their trauma was real, and they were believed, not shamed or silenced in the courtroom," Carrillo added. "They feel vindicated and will now focus on the much-needed healing the jury has provided for them."

Foppoli's attorney, Andrew Watters, said in a statement to Fox News Digital that he would seek a mistrial over claims that the court improperly excluded key witnesses for the defense. If that fails, Watters said he would pursue an appeal.

"What happened with the verdict was that the jury sent a message based on questionable self-reported evidence and junk science, and that’s not appropriate. It appears the passions of the jury were inflamed by the evidence, and they hated my client, so they made a very large award to punish and make an example of him," Watters said in a statement.

Foppoli, speaking at a press conference outside the courthouse Friday, said his accusers "are trying to crucify me for a cause I'm not responsible for," adding that they were motivated by the $13 million payout.

Foppoli still faces a separate lawsuit from Farrah Abraham, a social media influencer and former reality television personality who claims the ex-politician raped her in March 2021 at a house party in Florida. That civil case is expected to go to trial next year, according to court records.

The Chronicle reported that Christopher Creek Winery, which Foppoli owns, settled a separate lawsuit filed by a Montana woman who alleged Foppoli raped her multiple times in 2020 when she was 18.

item.content:encoded:
The college football season is humming along, and Friday night's action between the Kansas Jayhawks and the Missouri Tigers gifted us some must-see early season fireworks.

Things got hot and heavy before the game even started, with Kansas dropping a hype video in the lead-up to the game that framed the Tigers as "evil," alluding to Missouri's involvement as a slave state in the mid 1800s.

Mizzou got the last laugh, though, as the Tigers blasted the Jayhawks 38-21, adding a late score that head coach Eli Drinkwitz said was meant to "embarrass" their rivals for their social media stunt.

All of that is well and good, and it's what makes college football the greatest sport on earth, but that's not why we are here.

item.title: Nighttime bathroom trips could reveal hidden health issues — here's when to worry
item.description: Nocturia affects half of adults over 50, but experts say frequent nighttime urination could signal sleep apnea, diabetes or an enlarged prostate.
item.content:encoded:
Getting out of bed once during the night to use the bathroom is common, but repeated trips could signal underlying issues, health experts warn.

Waking up more than once a night to urinate can meet the clinical definition of nocturia, which affects about half of adults over 50 and becomes more common with age, according to a recent StudyFinds report. The International Continence Society’s formal definition of nocturia includes even one nighttime trip, but frequency, disruption and a change from a person’s usual pattern all matter.

"Everyone has a baseline of what’s normal urinary frequency for them," Dr. Ali Dabaja, a urologist at Henry Ford Health in Michigan, told the outlet. "But if you wake at least twice to go to the bathroom during eight hours of sleep, that’s considered nocturia."

DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID

Nocturia isn't simply a bladder issue, according to Dr. Jeffrey Chester, a licensed physician and medical director of The Ohana Luxury Addiction Treatment Center in Hawaii.

"A change in nighttime urinary patterns is definitely worth mentioning to a physician or healthcare provider, especially when it begins suddenly, becomes more frequent, or disrupts a person's sleep," Chester told Fox News Digital.

Alcohol and caffeine intake, the amount and timing of fluid consumption, and certain medications can all contribute, he added.

JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS

Waking up once isn't a cause for concern, agreed Catherine Darley, a naturopathic doctor and founder of Skilled Sleeper in Seattle, but more than once can be "concerning," she told Fox News Digital.

Experts note that it can raise the risk of falls, especially for those with mobility or balance challenges. Research shows two or more nightly trips to the bathroom are linked to a higher risk of fall-related injuries, StudyFinds reported.

Sleep disorders can also be a factor, Darley said, including obstructive sleep apnea, which can affect hormones involved in suppressing urine production overnight. Restless legs syndrome could also contribute to nighttime urination and is more common with age, Darley added.

OLDER ADULTS TAKING 5 OR MORE PRESCRIPTION DRUGS FACE HIGHER RISK OF DEATH, STUDY FINDS

She advised starting with your primary care provider to look for an underlying cause, and checking in with doctors and pharmacists to see if medications could be involved in frequent bathroom trips. In some cases, they could adjust the timing to prevent late-night wake-ups.

Other issues could be the cause, too, according to StudyFinds, including diabetes, an overactive bladder, an enlarged prostate and fluid buildup.

For some people, simple habits can help, including not drinking for roughly two hours before bedtime and stopping alcohol about three hours before bed, Darley said.

She also suggested keeping floors clear of rugs and clutter, using gentle amber lighting, sitting on the edge of the bed before standing to avoid getting dizzy and installing grab bars for extra support.

item.title: Mackenzie Phillips shocks with 15-year celibacy confession as Sharon Stone, Teri Hatcher rethink romance
item.description: Mackenzie Phillips revealed on a podcast that she has been celibate for 15 years, joining Sharon Stone and Teri Hatcher in new Hollywood trend.
item.content:encoded:
Mackenzie Phillips revealed that her past extroverted life is nothing like her current status.

Phillips, 66, admitted in an upcoming episode of Valerie Bertinelli's "Getting Naked" podcast that her social battery quickly becomes depleted after a busy day.

"I would get home, and I would have no words left, you know, and so in order to get up and do it again the next day, I had to be alone to recharge," she said, per People. "Which is, by the way, why — am I going to say this out loud? — I have been celibate for 15 years."

'AMERICAN PIE' STAR SHANNON ELIZABETH SWEARS OFF DATING, SAYS ONLYFANS IS 'THE ONLY RELATIONSHIP I NEED'

Bertinelli confided that "there was nothing wrong with being celibate," before Phillips explained that she's "had enough sex to last for several lifetimes for several people."

"And the parts of me that were injured or wounded, I can care for them myself," she said before noting that she doesn't date. "I have my little friend in the bedside drawer."

Bertinelli admitted that she also experienced "periods of celibacy" and hasn't been physically intimate in "almost two years now."

Phillips first married music manager Jeff Sessler for two years before their divorce in 1981. She then married guitarist Shane Fontayne for 14 years before their split in 2000.

SHARON STONE ADMITS THE BRUTAL MOMENT SHE KNEW HER MARRIAGE WAS OVER

In 2005, the "American Graffiti" actress married her third husband, Keith Levenson, which ended in divorce two years later.

Celibacy appeared to be trending in Hollywood this summer as Sharon Stone recently admitted that she, too, chose a path of celibacy.

"I'm a really good girlfriend, but I haven't been a girlfriend in a long time," Stone said during an appearance on the "Mayim Bialik's Breakdown" podcast. "And I've been a girlfriend to bad boyfriends, and I've been a girlfriend to good boyfriends."

CHRISTIE BRINKLEY SAYS SHE'S RETHINKING SOULMATES AFTER FOUR MARRIAGES

"I've had good luck and bad luck and no luck at all," she said. "For quite a long time I’ve had no luck at all. I've been celibate for quite a while now because I'm just at the point where I really only want to be with someone that I care for."

While the "Basic Instinct" star revealed her dating patterns, she also noted that she's now looking for "someone that's my companion, not just someone to have sex with."

"I'm kind of bored with that," Stone said of casual flings. "I'm in the no luck at all phase right now," before adding that it's "the phase you need to be willing to be in to have the thing that I really want."

Bialik asked if Stone had "a great love" of her life. The "Total Recall" star was first married to producer Michael Greenburg for six years before their divorce in 1990. She was then married to journalist Phil Bronstein from 1998 to 2004.

"I have had loves in my life, but I don't think I've had the great love of my life," she said.

"Desperate Housewives" actress Teri Hatcher recently confessed that she hasn't been on a date in seven years.

Hatcher, 61, told HELLO! that while she would "never say never" to a date, she's absolutely "so single."

"Oh my god, I'm so single. I go through life with an open heart and I would never say never, but I don't date," she confessed earlier this week. "I don't go on dates, I don't look to go on dates. I haven't been on a date in… I don't think I'm exaggerating if I say seven years."

Hatcher added, "I have such a giant community of beautiful friends and most of my girlfriends who are my age I've known for at least 30 years, and they're mostly married."

While she did briefly date a British man, Hatcher admitted that there "really isn't a new source of people."

"People would say... 'Are you dating?' and I'd say, 'Well, I don't date much anymore because I used to date, and you'd look across the table at the guy... you'd think, 'OK, I wonder if we're going to end up in bed together,'" she said.

"You know, I thought, I'm going to say to the universe that I am open and vulnerable, and I'm putting myself out there," Hatcher explained on "Getting Grilled with Curtis Stone."

She added, "Well, they thought I was pretending to be Teri Hatcher."

"They apologized, and then I was like, 'I'm sort of over it.' So now I'm over it," she continued. "I'm definitely done with the dating apps, and I feel like if there's any way I'll go somewhere and meet someone, that's what it's going to have to be, but honestly, I'm happy."

item.title: Iowa supervisor slams ban on guaranteed income programs as state ‘waging ideological wars’
item.description: Mandi Remington says Iowa's state ban on guaranteed income programs blocks local governments from testing direct cash payments to fight poverty.
item.content:encoded:
A local elected official in Iowa is criticizing state lawmakers after they blocked cities and counties from testing direct cash payments to residents, claiming local governments are being handcuffed by state-level "ideological wars."

Mandi Remington, a Democratic county supervisor in Johnson County, Iowa, told Fox News Digital that she wanted to test whether giving cash to low-income residents could serve as a feasible poverty-alleviation policy. However, the effort was shut down before it could launch.

"We are supposedly a home rule state, but that's not what it seems like in practice," Remington said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "I live in a blue dot in a red state and, essentially, anything that we try to do in these pockets that is not being done in other parts of the state automatically gets pushed back against."

Remington’s comments follow an op-ed she wrote arguing that guaranteed income programs "help everyday Iowans." She noted that the Johnson County Board of Supervisors attempted to bring a guaranteed income initiative to their community, championed by Supervisor V Fixmer-Oraiz.

ALBUQUERQUE USES WEED TAX TO FUND 'NO-STRINGS-ATTACHED' GUARANTEED INCOME, SPARKING POLICY DEBATE

The local push was inspired by similar pilots across the country, including the UpLift trial in central Iowa, which provided 110 families with $500 per month for two years. Remington argued the policy would build on successes seen in other jurisdictions.

Those plans were derailed when Iowa Republicans passed legislation prohibiting local governments from creating or maintaining guaranteed income programs. Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds signed House File 2319 into law on May 1, 2024. Proponents of the ban, including GOP lawmakers, argued that government cash handouts undermine the American work ethic, subsidize low wages, and foster government dependency.

"There's no room for doing research. There's no room for evaluating evidence. There's no interest in even hearing about evidence that has been found in other places," Remington told Fox News Digital. "I have not been present on the universal income matter specifically at the Capitol, but I have testified in legislative hearings here and watched as legislators didn't even pretend to listen to the people speaking to them. Because in their minds, whether they want to call it socialist or leftist or whatever term they throw at it, they have just lumped it into a certain ideological category because of where it's coming from."

GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAM TARGETS LOW-INCOME HOMES LED BY BLACK MOMS AS CASH HANDOUTS SURGE NATIONWIDE

In her published letter, Remington argued that restricting local control hurts working families.

"Unfortunately, some of our state leaders are more interested in controlling local government and waging ideological wars than they are in passing policies that help everyday Iowans," Remington wrote. "The state’s ban on guaranteed income isn’t good policy, and it doesn’t help hard-working Iowans get by. It’s simply obstructionism without evidence. Seven Republican legislators understood this and joined Democrats in voting against the ban."

Gov. Reynolds' office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. 

Iowa is far from the only state where Republicans have pushed back against cash-handout initiatives.

GOP lawmakers across the country have raised legal, budgetary and philosophical concerns regarding guaranteed basic income. In Michigan, House Republicans demanded a rigorous inspection of a taxpayer-funded cash assistance program for new mothers, questioning its benefits and scrutinizing how millions in public funds were spent.

In Texas, Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Harris County — home to Houston — over its guaranteed income program, leading the Texas Supreme Court to freeze the trial. Meanwhile, in Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a Republican-led bill that would have prohibited local governments from enacting guaranteed income programs.

MICHIGAN LAWMAKER MOVES TO SHUT DOWN 'GUARDRAIL-FREE' CASH HANDOUT PROGRAM FOR NEW MOTHERS

Progressive groups have pushed back against state-level restrictions. Adriane Brown, senior communications director for the Economic Security Project (ESP) — an advocacy organization founded in 2016 to promote direct cash transfer policies — defended the trials.

"It doesn’t serve anyone to ban guaranteed income. Mandi Remington’s letter speaks to the precarity — emotional, financial and otherwise — of leaving an abusive relationship," Brown told Fox News Digital. "Thankfully, there are several guaranteed income pilots across the country building on what we know about cash’s ability to offer survivors stability during these difficult transitions."

The ESP helped create over 100 guaranteed income pilots across the U.S.

"In the case of Iowa specifically, thankfully, not all lawmakers fell along partisan lines," Brown added. "If elected officials’ end goal is truly to make sure families are safe and secure, then guaranteed income pilots should be allowed to exist. Lawmakers who voted to ban guaranteed income amid a cost-of-living crisis are out of touch and do not care about families."

Beyond political opposition, many guaranteed income programs face an impending funding cliff. Dozens of cities launched cash-transfer pilots using federal pandemic relief funds from the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA). Under federal rules, ARPA allocations had to be legally obligated by the end of 2024 and fully spent by December 31, 2026.

As federal relief funds dry up, local leaders are scrambling to find alternative funding streams. While Cook County, Illinois — the second-largest county in the nation — moved to set up ongoing municipal funding for guaranteed income following its initial 2022 pilot, most local jurisdictions lack the budget to sustain direct cash transfers without private philanthropy or federal aid.

"The UpLift program was able to find a way to sustain itself through non-government money," Remington told Fox News Digital. "Unfortunately, we are also now in a position where all of our nonprofit agencies and mutual aid organizations are in their own financial crises as well. So funding in general has become a problem across the board for government, private citizens, and community agencies."

item.title: Bill Maher rips Macklemore's Gaza stance, says celebrity 'moral confusion' is fueling antisemitism
item.description: Bill Maher targeted Macklemore on Rosh Hashanah for calling the Gaza war a genocide, arguing that the claim fuels a global rise in antisemitism.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Bill Maher spent the first night of Rosh Hashanah taking aim at Macklemore and other anti-Israel celebrities, arguing that calling the war in Gaza a genocide is fueling a global rise in antisemitism.

During Friday night’s episode of HBO’s "Real Time," Maher first criticized members of the Democratic Party who have spoken out against Israel during the Israel-Hamas war.

"Because nowhere has this moral confusion become more obvious than in a place called Gaza," Maher said. "A little strip of land that was not part of the original Israel, but they won in a war launched against them, but then gave back, gave back as a peace gesture — did they tell you that part on TikTok, kids?"

BILL MAHER BLASTS DEMOCRATIC PARTY, SAYS IT IS FINE WITH RELIGION 'AS LONG AS THAT FAITH ISN’T JEWISH'

Maher then turned his attention to Macklemore — whose real name is Benjamin Hammond Haggerty — after the musician repeatedly made calls to "Free Palestine" while performing his anti-Israel song "Hind's Hall" as an opening act for Ed Sheeran at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, earlier this month.

"I think Macklemore spoke for all clueless celebrities when he said, ‘I know enough to know this is a genocide,’" Maher continued. "Actually, you don't know s---. It's not. It's not a genocide. It's a counterattack in a war."

MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER

The "Thrift Shop" rapper made headlines in early September for his comments about the Israel-Hamas war while on stage at the concert, where he wore a keffiyeh as he delivered his message to the crowd.

"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine," Macklemore said.

JERRY SEINFELD GIVES BLUNT THREE-WORD RESPONSE TO INFLUENCER ASKING FOR A 'FREE PALESTINE'

"I said, ‘Free Palestine!’ I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them," he continued.

Fox News Digital reached out to Macklemore's representatives for comment.

Maher continued criticizing Macklemore and other liberal figures, disputing their assertion that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza in response to Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

"Gaza equals genocide is a lie, an easily provable lie," Maher said. "And the fact that so many prominent Democrats go along with it is, to me, the party's worst moment since they undid Reconstruction after the Civil War. Democrats are policing their candidates really hard on this issue. Say it — say it's a genocide. Say it."

PROMINENT HOLOCAUST MUSEUM CHALLENGES MAMDANI WITH OFFER IN RESPONSE TO CLAIMS ABOUT 'GENOCIDE' IN GAZA

Maher concluded his "New Rule" segment by arguing that what he described as false claims about the war have contributed to the rise of antisemitism.

"If you're one of the many people these days asking, ‘This explosion of antisemitism around the world that we see, where is it coming from?’" Maher said. "This. This is where it's coming from. Because if you really think someone is committing genocide, of course you have full permission to hate them. And history shows, for whatever reason, when it comes to hating the Jews, people don't need a lot of permission."

GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS

Macklemore’s comments also drew criticism from Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, who told Fox News Digital that the rapper's public stance on Israel represents a "calculated risk."

"Take a political stance and most celebrities can count on alienating half their audience," Mudd said. "That's the easy math. The harder split is what's left: about a third thinks you should stay in your lane and entertain, and only a third is glad you used your platform to say it."

"It's fine, if you're making a calculated risk," he continued. "Using your platform to influence politics is a decision that can affect your fans' support, your reputation, your career, and your future earnings, so know the risk before you make it."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Mudd concluded his comments by suggesting that Macklemore should take into account the potential consequences of taking such a polarizing stance as a public figure.

"If Macklemore were my client, I'd advise him that calling a war a genocide invites the public shredding Bill Maher just delivered," Mudd told Fox News Digital. "There's no rule against entertainers taking a stance, but he needs to understand the career, reputational and pushback risk that comes with it."

item.title: Tragedy at sea leaves teen stranded on overturned boat for nearly 3 days in frigid waters
item.description: A 15-year-old boy survived for nearly three days atop an overturned fishing boat in the Bering Sea before a Coast Guard pilot spotted him at the right moment.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Coast Guard pulled off a compelling rescue this week.

The rescue, which unfolded Monday, was announced Wednesday.

A 15-year-old Alaska boy was found atop an overturned fishing boat — after nearly three days in the frigid waters of the Bering Sea. 

CLIMBER STRANDED ON 6-INCH LEDGE AT 11,000 FEET AS 46 MPH WINDS GROUND RESCUE HELICOPTER

The teen was found alive — with his teeth chattering — about 4 miles east of St. Lawrence Island, a remote island in the Bering Sea roughly 100 miles west of mainland Alaska and about 40 miles from Russia's Chukchi Peninsula, according to multiple reports, including from The Associated Press. 

His fishing vessel, last seen Friday departing Savoonga for St. Lawrence Island, had missed its scheduled return early Sunday morning.

The boy was the lone survivor after the other two people aboard the vessel — his 16-year-old brother and their 39-year-old cousin — perished.

The teen was experiencing symptoms of hypothermia when he was found, according to reports.

The fishing vessel Northwest Explorer rescued the boy after Coast Guard aircrews dropped a life raft and coordinated the recovery.

NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING'

Lt. Cmdr. Jonathon Resch, the Coast Guard pilot who located the teen, told ABC News that he and his team were "elated" to find him.

"People don't survive those scenarios," Resch said. 

"People don't flip boats and survive nights."

Resch also said he "just happen[ed] to be looking out the window at the right angle of sun" when he spotted the teen's raft, he told the same outlet.

The search involved the Coast Guard, the Alaska Rescue Coordination Center, the Alaska Air National Guard, Alaska State Troopers and local authorities — with multiple planes and helicopters deployed.

In a statement, Coast Guard Arctic District commander Rear Adm. Bob Little called the loss of the two mariners "tragic."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"We are grateful for the incredible efforts of the motor vessel Northwest Explorer, [plus] federal, state, village first responders and mission partners who assisted in the effort that resulted in a life saved," Little said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Coast Guard for further comment and details. 

The boy's mother was listening to a radio transmission of the rescue Monday while other family members huddled around a speakerphone, one of them told the AP.

"We all cried and jumped for joy when the captain announced on the radio, ‘We found a kid, he’s alive, he’s alive,’" the family member said. "Then we asked, ‘Where’s the rest of them?’"

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Video of the rescue shows the boy in a bright yellow jacket kneeling atop the overturned skiff. The boat’s crew tossed him a line, tugging the skiff closer until they could pull him into a rescue basket.

The bodies of his two deceased family members were recovered. 

Earlier this year, Fox News Digital reported on another dramatic rescue after a family of three was found alive following nearly a week adrift in the Pacific Ocean.

The family's boat engine failed — prompting a Coast Guard rescue.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

item.title: From football Saturdays to routine weekdays, the music never stops at this UT house full of college musicians
item.description: Anna Buendia's "Meet Me Here" program turns a University of Texas student house into a free jam session hub with live music every Sunday in Austin.
item.content:encoded:
There may be nothing more symbolic of campus culture at big American universities than a college football weekend.

The pomp, the circumstance, the parties, and of course, the big game itself, unify the community with a spirit and an electricity that is hard to replicate elsewhere.

But the arts, especially music, come close.

Later Saturday, as No. 1 Ohio State invades the Lone Star State to take on No. 4 Texas in the most marquee Week 2 matchup in the country, OutKick University’s Game Of The Week, students on campus in Austin will be revved up for some great football.

Music from the marching band, and from tailgating parties will be a big part of the festivities.

And the music won’t stop there.

If they want to keep the groove going for a post-game party on Sunday, Texas students are welcome, as they are every Sunday, to stop by Anna Buendia’s house, which is affectionately known as "The Lodge," located off Pearl Street on West Campus.

"The Lodge" is where music happens every day, and especially on Sundays, when musicians play all day long and free food is provided to anyone who stops by.

"It's Austin, so music's everywhere ," Buendia said. "It’s a densely art-rich city to be in, and just finding a microculture within it has been so wonderful. "

EVEN ON OPENING WEEKEND, FOOTBALL PLAYERS AT CLEMSON, LSU MIGHT BE UPSTAGED ON CAMPUS BY THESE FURRY FRIENDS

Buendia, a Texas native who has been either writing or performing music since she was 16, is one of five roommates at "The Lodge." All of the roommates in the rented home, steps from the heart of campus, are musicians who love to write music, play music and perform music together.

And, as a way to spread their love of music, they have opened up their home, which is equipped with all kinds of instruments and equipment, to other Texas students for free jam sessions, rehearsals, writing sessions and even more slickly produced ticketed performances.

The program that Buendia created is called "Meet Me Here." As in, meet me here…to make music (or just listen to it).

"I kind of became obsessed with understanding the creative processes of the musicians around me," Buendia, a 21-year-old senior public relations major said. "Everyone has a really interesting process to their work. What I wanted to do was, it started out of my bedroom, and so that was the concept (to) meet me in my creative sanctuary. And I wanted to meet the artists in their creative plane to understand the processes for their works. And I kept saying that. I kept saying, I just want them to meet me here, meet me here. That's how that started. Meet me here."

In the living room of "The Lodge," Buendia says that there are 20 guitars, two drum sets and a sound system. Students will reserve their "Meet Me Here" space to practice their songs, to play with others, to have fun.

"Our whole living room is perfect for a rehearsal space, and so daily, there's rehearsals happening," Buendia said. "Even when there's not rehearsals happening, there's music being made. Like yesterday, I had a small moment of bliss. I was just walking down my stairs, and I could hear my roommate upstairs recording a song, and two of my roommates downstairs, each learning and writing songs, like separate from each other, and it was just like, wow, like it's really awesome to see that."

The house is also used for public performances, from small intimate gatherings any day of the week, to the outdoor Sunday staple that entertains and feeds the neighborhood in a block-party setting.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"We do these ‘Meet Me Here’ tapings. Basically, it's like a whole production," Buendia said. "We bring a whole production crew, and the living room turns into a set, and we have an intimate audience of 25 to 30 people upstairs on our second-floor balcony. And we do a live taping of a local band, and it's a very intimate event. Normally, ticket purchasers get a piece of physical media, and we try to keep the tickets as cheap as possible. Then the artist gets rights to all the audio and the video that we take, and all of that work from our production crew is done for free, just out of passion for the space and the artists that we're highlighting."

The Sunday Jams started as something small and casual, too. But they have evolved into a community outreach that includes clothing drives and other charitable initiatives.

"I started grilling hot dogs outside my house on Sundays, and putting my instruments outside with my roommates, and we would just do like free hot dogs, come jam with us. And it became like a consistent Sunday thing," Buendia said. "I collaborated with a mutual aid organization founded by a good friend called the 'Student Solidarity Network.' They have helped us build just an incredible community of our neighbors that cook biweekly food for like 100 to 200 people. It's a different menu every week. They bring laborers to help us move all the equipment outside and set up the stage. We do (clothing) drives, so if you have any clothes you need to donate, you can bring it to our house, and we have free piles and racks of clothes at every Sunday jam.

"It’s a biweekly block party. Anyone can come join, hop on the mic, on the drums, on the guitar, on the bass, eat, just sit there. There's something happening here every single day, music related."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Buendia also sees friendships form and partnerships born. Students find bandmates and singing partners and learn from each other.

"I always like to hear a conversation when we start wrapping up where a musician asks someone that they just met that day, ‘Do you wanna come to my place and record a song? ’ And, and it's always like, ‘Yes, of course,’ and then they come back next week together, and it's just, it's a really beautiful thing to watch. So there are opportunities. I think just like the same way connecting with anyone in any other way, there are opportunities to grow mutually."

Now in her final year of college, Buendia has seen plenty of growth in herself. In all kinds of ways.

But she is convinced that her music, "Meet Me Here" and "The Lodge" are the biggest reasons she let down her guard and was able to maximize her college experience.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

"Yesterday, I was reading through my old journals from my freshman year of high school talking about how I felt so lonely those first few months, and I was just thinking about if I was able to walk upon (Pearl) street on a Sunday, it would have done so much for me," Buendia said. "It feels really beautiful that I'm able to be part of such a fruitful community that cares about each other and is interested in setting up events where people can be accepted and fed and clothed and walk away with a full belly, a new t-shirt, hopefully new shoes, pants, and, just knowing that they have somewhere where they belong. "

To check out the music at "The Lodge" at the University of Texas, follow Buendia and her "Meet Me Here" friends on social media.

item.title: The one line from JD Vance’s GOP keynote that reveals his vision for America
item.description: JD Vance framed the midterm elections as a fight over every American child's birthright in a Dallas keynote that previewed his post-Trump GOP vision.
item.content:encoded:
Vice President JD Vance used his keynote address at the Republican midterm convention Thursday to frame the November elections as a fight over America’s future, arguing that every child is entitled to inherit the country’s opportunities regardless of background.

The speech also gave Vance one of his most prominent national platforms since becoming vice president to define his own political vision, as he emerges as a central figure in the GOP’s post-Trump future and speculation continues about a potential 2028 presidential campaign.

"Every American child is born an heir, born with the right to inherit the blessings of the greatest country on Earth — not because of who their parents are, what they look like or where they come from, but because they are Americans and this is our country," Vance said in Dallas.

"And that birthright, ladies and gentlemen, is what this November is all about," he added.

VANCE, CRUZ, HEAD TO IOWA ON 2026 MISSIONS AS 2028 GOP RACE TO SUCCEED TRUMP HEATS UP

Vance tied that idea to his own family, speaking about the birth of his fourth child, Alec, six weeks ago. He said he wants his son and all American children to grow up with access to clean water, healthy food, a quality education, safe communities and the opportunity to afford a home and raise a family.

He also connected that vision to the legacy of his late friend Charlie Kirk, who was killed one year ago. Vance said Kirk encouraged young men to fall in love, start families and become fathers.

The speech marked a shift from the personal story of Vance’s Appalachian upbringing that he emphasized during the 2024 Republican convention. Instead, Vance presented himself as a father focused on the country his children will inherit, while using the platform to preview the issues and themes that could define his future in the Republican Party.

TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE

Vance then pivoted from his family-focused message to a sweeping attack on the Democratic Party. He accused Democrats of abandoning working-class Americans and becoming increasingly hostile toward the country’s traditional values.

"The Democrats are the party of hatred," Vance said. "They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it."

FOLLOW FOX NEWS DIGITAL’S COVERAGE OF THE GOP’S 2026 MIDTERM CONVENTION

He urged Republicans to view the November election as more than a traditional partisan contest.

"This November is so much more than red team versus blue team," Vance said. "It’s about fighting for our fellow citizens, for their dreams, and for the inheritance of a great nation that all of us are going to leave behind."

The speech placed family, faith and national identity at the center of Vance’s midterm message while offering a glimpse of how he could define himself within the Republican Party beyond President Donald Trump.

item.title: Ted Cruz got booed so loudly during 'College GameDay' interview you couldn't hear a thing he said
item.description: Ted Cruz was booed so loudly during his "College GameDay" appearance in Austin that his pitch for the "Save College Sports Act" was nearly drowned out.
item.content:encoded:
Nothing says college football like Ted Cruz and Rece Davis.

Or, you know, something like that.

Cruz made a nearly 10-minute cameo on ESPN's College GameDay Saturday morning to push the "Protect College Sports Act," which is currently collecting dust in Congress. Among the many things Cruz said, the most notable was this:

"I think we're going to get the (60) votes."

PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT STALLS IN OVERNIGHT SENATE SHOWDOWN, VOTE PUSHED TO SEPTEMBER AFTER CHAOTIC EVENING

Before we get into the nuts and bolts of the bill — and believe me, I'll keep that brief — we have to address the elephant in the room.

Cruz, a Texas senator, got booed so loudly during the entirety of the interview — which took place on the Longhorns' Austin campus — that you could barely hear a word he said.

Fair is fair, and I have to be fair here ...

This was a tough watch:

Goodness gracious. Just a brutal scene here for Ted Cruz. You couldn't hear a thing he said, for the most part, the entire interview. At one point, it sounded like it was finally dying down, only for the "Ted you suck" chants to take over.

Now, I have no idea why they were booing Ted Cruz. The truth is, they don't, either. Do you think a bunch of hungover college kids who haven't slept since Thursday give a you-know-what about the "Protect College Sports Act"?

Of course not! They couldn't tell you one single thing in the act, or what it's about, or whether it's good or not. They're not booing the bill itself — which, in theory, will help stabilize the current NIL landscape in college sports, which has spiraled out of control.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Nick Saban has backed it. Deion Sanders was on a commercial supporting the bill immediately following Cruz's appearance.

PRESIDENT TRUMP PUSHES LAWMAKERS ON LEGISLATION AS 'PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT' HANGS ON BY A THREAD

Still, it's struggling to pass. Shocking! That almost never happens in Congress.

As for the booing ... I assume it's because Cruz A) is a Republican and college campuses lean left, B) students don't want politics on a sports show, C) Austin is a liberal town, or C) all the above.

TED CRUZ URGES SENATE TO STAY IN WASHINGTON UNTIL PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT PASSES THIS WEEK

He's clearly a Longhorns fan, so you would think that would've been his saving grace here. But not in Austin, which is a liberal haven in a deep red state.

Credit to ESPN for having a Republican on its airwaves, though. That's a big step!

Just wish we could've heard a thing he said.

item.title: 153 million driver's license scans may be on the dark web
item.description: A dark web service called Nexus claimed to hold over 153 million driver's license records, and the FBI confirms it is now looking into the incident.
item.content:encoded:
Think about how often you hand someone your driver's license without giving it much thought. You rent a car, check into a business or go somewhere that needs to verify your age. Someone scans your ID, hands it back and you move on.

A dark web service called Nexus claimed to have collected more than 153 million driver's license records from people in the United States and Canada. It also claimed to have more than 10 million identification cards, over 3 million travel documents or international IDs and at least 579,000 medical cards. That's a staggering amount of identity information.

There is an important caveat, though. The 153 million figure comes from Nexus itself. It has not been confirmed as the number of unique people affected. Some records also contained multiple images of the same license. Still, researchers found enough real driver's licenses in the database to get the FBI's attention.

You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed.
